ref: Hauler 1900 (Didascaliae apostolorum fragmenta Veronensia Latina), 'Canonum reliquiae' (Canones Aegyptiorum), canon LXXIII, printed p. 110. Verona Latin, NOT the Apostolic Tradition itself; Hauler cross-refers it to Tattam c. 46, Lagarde AA p. 467-469, Achelis p. 97-102, Rahmani II c. 8-10
greek: manum habens in caput eius inpositam baptizet semel. Et postea dicat: 'Credis in Chr(istu)m Ie(su)m, filium D(e)i, qui natus est de sp(irit)u s(an)c(t)o ex Maria uirgine et crucifixus sub Pontio Pilato et mortuus est et sepultus et resurrexit die tertia uiuus a mortuis et ascendit in caelis et sedit ad dexteram patris uenturus iudicare uiuos et mortuos?' Et cum ille dixerit: 'Credo', iterum baptizetur. Et iterum dicat: 'Credis in sp(irit)u s(an)c(t)o et sanctam ecclesiam et carnis
greek_edition: Hauler 1900, Latin (Verona), read from the Internet Archive scan hauler1900b.pdf, text layer (Scribe OCR). Margin note 'Sees (Achel' and line numbers removed; the quote is cut at 'carnis' (line break in the print). Original text is Latin, not Greek; the Greek of the Apostolic Tradition is lost.
english: Having laid his hand on his head, let him baptize him once. Then let him say: 'Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and died and was buried, and rose again alive from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father, to come to judge the living and the dead?' And when he has said 'I believe', let him be baptized again. And again let him say: 'Do you believe in the Holy Spirit and the holy Church and the resurrection of the flesh' [page 130 ends here; continuation on the next printed page not read].
page: Hauler printed p. 110 (canon LXXIII); PDF p. 130 of hauler1900b.pdf
edition: Edmund Hauler, Didascaliae Apostolorum fragmenta Veronensia Latina, Leipzig: Teubner, 1900 (Internet Archive copy didascaliaeapost0000edmu; Google copy didascaliaeapos00haulgoog)
what_it_says: The Latin Egyptian Canons (Verona) give a three-question baptismal interrogation (Christ, Holy Spirit and Church, resurrection), with triple immersion, parallel to Apostolic Tradition 21.
limits: The Verona text is the Egyptian Canons, a related but different church order, not the Apostolic Tradition. Its Latin is a translation from Arabic per Achelis and Horner's chain of versions; it does not establish the Greek wording of the AT. It names no author. The triadic structure is interrogatory, so it proves a Trinitarian baptismal pattern, not a doctrine of the Son's eternal generation. Opponents can say the Trinity here is only a sequence of three questions.

ref: Egyptian church order (Coptic 'Apostolical Constitutions or Canons of the Apostles'), Tattam's chapter on the institution of holy baptism (Hauler cites it as Tattam c. 46); printed p. 58 of Tattam 1848
greek_edition: Coptic original not copied (OCR of the Coptic side is unreliable). English read from the Internet Archive scan, text layer (PDF p. 89). Footnote marks (asterisk, 'f' after 'Trinity') removed.
english: I believe in the only true God, the Father Almighty, and in His only begotten Son Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, and in the Holy Spirit, the quickener; the Trinity, of the same essence; one Sovereignty, one Kingdom, one Faith, one Baptism; and in the Holy Catholic Apostolic Church, and in the life everlasting. Amen.
translator: Henry Tattam (Coptic edition and English translation)
page: printed p. 58; PDF p. 89 of TheApostolicalConstitutions.pdf
edition: Henry Tattam, The Apostolical Constitutions, or Canons of the Apostles, in Coptic, London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1848
what_it_says: The declared creed before immersion names the only true God the Father Almighty, the only begotten Son, the Holy Spirit, and 'the Trinity, of the same essence', then the Church and life everlasting.
limits: Tattam's footnote f reads 'Arab. the Trinity' (the Arabic has no 'of the same essence'), so the phrase is not in every witness. It is a Coptic church order of unknown date, not the Apostolic Tradition. The 'same essence' wording is probably a later Nicene-era phrase; this is an inference, not verified here.

ref: Tattam 1848 (Coptic church order), baptismal interrogations, printed pp. 58 and 60 (p. 59 is not in the text layer); Hauler's Verona canon LXXIII is cross-referenced to this chapter
greek_edition: Coptic not copied. English from the text layer of PDF pp. 89 and 91; PDF p. 90 (printed p. 59) shows only Coptic in the text layer. OCR 'see^K' read as 'seed'.
english: Dost thou believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God the Father; that he became man in a wonderful manner for us, in an incomprehensible unity, by his Holy Spirit, of Mary the Holy Virgin, without the seed of man; and that he [printed p. 59 not in the text layer] was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, and died of his own will once for our redemption, and rose on the third day, loosing the bonds (of death): he ascended up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of his good Father on high, and he cometh again to judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom? And dost thou believe in the Holy good Spirit, and quickener, who wholly purifieth in the Holy Church?
page: printed pp. 58 and 60 (PDF pp. 89 and 91); printed p. 59 unread
edition: Henry Tattam, The Apostolical Constitutions, or Canons of the Apostles, in Coptic, London, 1848
what_it_says: The second question names Christ and the Holy Spirit; the Church and resurrection come later, the creed being cut into three parts, as in Hauler's Verona canon.
limits: Tattam's rendering has a garbled OCR word ('see^K' for 'seed') and a gap at printed p. 59. The text is Coptic, not the Apostolic Tradition. The 'holy good Spirit' wording is an English rendering of the Coptic.

ref: Horner 1904, 'Translation of the Ethiopic text' (Ethiopic 'Statutes/Canons' form), printed pp. 153-154, the baptism section. Canon number not identified
greek_edition: Ethiopic not copied; only the English translation of Horner is given. Ethiopic text printed in the book is not read. OCR line number 'ao' (for 20) removed.
english: I believe in one God, the Father almighty, and in his only Son, our Lord and our Saviour Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, giver of life to all creation, the Trinity equal in Godhead, one Lord, and one Kingdom and one Faith and one Baptism, in the holy Church Catholic, and life eternal Amen.
translator: George William Horner (translation of the Ethiopic)
page: printed p. 153 (creed); p. 154 (interrogation); PDF pp. 200-201 of statutes_text.pdf
edition: G. W. Horner, The Statutes of the Apostles, or Canones Ecclesiastici, London: Williams & Norgate, 1904
what_it_says: The Ethiopic form has a creed in the first person ('I believe in one God') with 'the Trinity equal in Godhead', followed by the interrogation about Christ, Spirit and Church.
limits: Horner's 'equal in Godhead' is his English rendering of the Ethiopic; the Ethiopic word is not given here. The text is an Ethiopic church order, not the Apostolic Tradition. Horner's introduction (p. viii) says the authorship of Hippolytus cannot at present be determined.

ref: Horner 1904, 'Translation of the Saidic text' (Sahidic Coptic church order), printed pp. 317-318, the baptism section
greek_edition: Sahidic not copied. The Greek words in brackets are Horner's own glosses in his English, not witnesses of a Greek text. OCR 'm' for 'in' corrected in the English.
english: I believe in the only true God, the Father, the almighty (pantocrator) and his only (monogenes) Son Jesus the Christ, our Lord and our Saviour, and his Holy Spirit, giver of life to the universe, the Trinity of the same substance (trias en homoousion), one Godhead, one Lordship, one Kingdom, one Faith, one Baptism, in the Catholic (katholike) apostolic holy Church, life eternal. Amen.
translator: George William Horner (translation of the Sahidic)
page: printed p. 317 (creed); p. 318 (interrogation); PDF pp. 364-365 of statutes_text.pdf
edition: G. W. Horner, The Statutes of the Apostles, London: Williams & Norgate, 1904
what_it_says: The Sahidic creed says 'the Trinity of the same substance' (Horner's gloss 'trias en homoousion'), a Nicene-style phrase in a Coptic baptismal creed.
limits: This is the phrase at issue for the Nicene question: it appears in the Coptic, but the Ethiopic (H6-04) has 'equal in Godhead' instead. The date of the phrase is not established here. The Greek glosses are Horner's own. The text is not the Apostolic Tradition.

ref: Horner 1904, Introduction, printed p. viii (the authorship question for the Canons and the Ethiopic/Arabic church orders)
greek_edition: English only; the Arabic/Ethiopic is not copied
english: Lastly, in Arabic are extant the Canons of Hippolytus and Constitutions by Hippolytus, whose name is found besides in the Ethiopic, derived probably from the Arabic. How far the authorship of Hippolytus is to be accepted cannot at present be determined, the chief interest of the name consists in the additional evidence which it gives for a Western origin of the canons.
page: printed p. viii; PDF p. 13 of statutes_text.pdf
edition: G. W. Horner, The Statutes of the Apostles, London, 1904
what_it_says: Horner says the Canons and Constitutions are attributed to Hippolytus in Arabic and Ethiopic, but that his authorship cannot yet be decided.
limits: Horner (1904) is an old source; the views of Brent, Bradshaw-Johnson-Phillips and Dix were not read here. The point is about the Arabic/Ethiopic Canons of Hippolytus, not the Apostolic Tradition.

ref: Horner 1904, Introduction, printed p. xiii: comparison of the Oblation prayer and doxology in the Ethiopic form with Hauler's Verona fragment (the Apostolic Tradition ch. 4 parallel)
english: E. alone of the three has the prayer of the Oblation, which however appears in Hauler's fragment with very slight variation, e.g., 'lead forth the holy ones' for 'justos inluminet'; adding 'on the night in which he was betrayed,' 'for the remission of sin,' 'having given thanks,' 'take and drink of it'; concluding with almost the same doxology in which 'the holy church' is inserted, which was omitted by the fragment in the prayer for the bishop.
page: printed p. xiii; PDF p. 18 of statutes_text.pdf
edition: G. W. Horner, The Statutes of the Apostles, London, 1904
what_it_says: Horner notes that the Ethiopic has the Oblation prayer, which also appears in Hauler's Verona fragment, and that its closing doxology adds 'the holy church', which the Verona fragment lacks in the prayer for the bishop.
limits: This is Horner's comparison, not the Apostolic Tradition's ch. 4 doxology itself. The doxology wording ('through Thy Son... in the holy church') is not quoted from the AT here. Dix's text was not read.

ref: Testamentum Domini nostri Jesu Christi (Syriac), Rahmani 1899, Latin translation, Liber III 'De collatione baptismi', printed p. 129
greek: Cum itaque baptizandus descenderit in aquas, baptizans manum ei imponens dicat ita: «Credzs 2m Deum, Patrem omnipotentem?» et baptizandus respondeat: Cedo. Et continuo ilum prima vice baptizet.
greek_edition: Latin (Rahmani's translation from the Syriac; the Syriac original is not copied). Quoted as printed in the OCR text layer of rahmani_text.pdf: 'Credzs 2m Deum' is OCR for 'Credis in Deum', 'Cedo' for 'Credo', 'ilum' for 'illum'. Verify against the scan.
english: When the candidate has gone down into the water, the baptizer lays his hand on him and says: 'Do you believe in God, the Father almighty?' And the candidate answers: 'I believe.' And at once he baptizes him the first time.
page: printed p. 129; PDF p. 190 of rahmani_text.pdf
edition: Ignatius Ephraem II Rahmani, Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi, Moguntiae: Kirchheim, 1899
what_it_says: The Syriac church order has the same three-part interrogatory baptism (God the Father; Christ Jesus; Spirit and Church), with triple immersion, parallel to AT 21.
limits: Syriac text (the original) is not read; Rahmani's Latin is a translation, and the OCR is unreliable. The Testamentum Domini is a Syriac church order, not the Apostolic Tradition; its relation to the AT is disputed (not settled here).

ref: Rahmani 1899, Latin commentary, 'De immersione', printed p. 217 (Testamentum Domini, Liber III, commentary)
greek: Procul dubio est ad trinam immersionem fuisse evangelicam formam prolatam. Ceteris autem notamus his haberi prototypum symboli fidei sub formula tamen interrogatoria, cujus quidem symboli partes respondent ad amussim symbolo dicto apostolorum, quo ecclesia romana utitur, exceptis duobus ultimis articulis, quorum alter refertur ad remissionem peccatorum, alter ad resurrectionem mortuorum.
greek_edition: Latin (Rahmani's commentary), text layer of rahmani_text.pdf (OCR). The footnote number '17120' printed inside the text was cut; 'immer- sionem' is joined.
english: Clearly the Gospel form was given for triple immersion. We note moreover that the prototype of the creed of faith is held here under an interrogatory form, whose parts correspond exactly to the apostles' creed used by the Roman church, except the last two articles, one of which refers to the forgiveness of sins, the other to the resurrection of the dead.
page: printed p. 217; PDF p. 278 of rahmani_text.pdf
edition: Ignatius Ephraem II Rahmani, Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi, Moguntiae: Kirchheim, 1899
what_it_says: Rahmani argues the interrogatory baptismal creed is a prototype of the Roman creed lacking the forgiveness and resurrection articles, which were not yet in the baptismal profession.
limits: Rahmani's argument is a 1899 view on the early creed, not a proof of Hippolytan authorship. It uses the Syriac text, not the Apostolic Tradition.

ref: Achelis, Die Canones Hippolyti (TU 6.4), 1891, Kapitel VII 'Zeit, Ort, Autor', printed pp. 212-213. The 'Canones Hippolyti' are an Arabic/Ethiopic church order, not the Apostolic Tradition
greek: Der Kopf der C. H. lautet: 'In nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti, Dei unici. Hi sunt canones ecclesiae et praecepta, quae scripsit Hippolytus, princeps episcoporum Romanorum secundum mandata apostolorum'
greek_edition: German monograph with Latin from the Arabic manuscript superscription (Rieu's catalogue). Read from the text layer of the Internet Archive scan; OCR. Not Greek.
english: The heading of the Canones Hippolyti reads: 'In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God. These are the canons of the church and the precepts that Hippolytus, chief of the bishops of Rome, wrote according to the commands of the apostles.' Achelis judges that this superscription cannot be trusted: 'chief of the bishops of Rome' (that is, patriarch of Rome) is an impossibility for that time.
translator: own translation (from Achelis's German and the Latin superscription)
page: printed pp. 212-213; PDF pp. 222-223 of diecanoneshippol00hipp.pdf
edition: Hans Achelis, Die Canones Hippolyti (Texte und Untersuchungen 6.4), Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1891
what_it_says: Achelis holds that the superscription naming Hippolytus as Roman bishop is not reliable evidence, although the title 'canons of the church and precepts' may be authentic.
limits: The superscription is for the Arabic Canons of Hippolytus, not for the Apostolic Tradition. Achelis' view is one 1891 scholar's view; Brent, Bradshaw-Johnson-Phillips and Dix are not read here.

ref: Achelis 1891, Kapitel VII, printed p. 215 (the attribution of the Canones to Hippolytus; the text went Greek > Coptic > Arabic > Latin)
greek: Tradition, welche auf Hippolyt fuhrt, kann nur dann Wert er- lialten, wenn sie durch andere, gewichtige Griinde unterstiitzt wird. Zunachst mussen wir uns an die Daten halten, welche der Inhalt der C. H. an die Hand giebt.
greek_edition: German, OCR text layer of the Internet Archive scan (diecanoneshippol00hipp_djvu.txt / PDF p. 225). Not Greek. Quoted as printed: 'fuhrt' = führt, 'er- lialten' = erhalten, 'Griinde' = Gründe, 'unterstiitzt' = unterstützt (OCR of umlauts).
english: The tradition that leads to Hippolytus can keep its value only if it is supported by other weighty reasons. First we must keep to the data that the content of the Canones gives. (Achelis adds on the same page that the text passed through three translations, from Greek into Coptic, from Coptic into Arabic and from Arabic into Latin, and was reworked by many additions.)
page: printed p. 215; PDF p. 225 of diecanoneshippol00hipp.pdf
edition: Hans Achelis, Die Canones Hippolyti, Leipzig, 1891
what_it_says: Achelis says the attribution to Hippolytus is accepted only on trust unless independent arguments support it, and that the text is a chain of translations with interpolations.
limits: Achelis' argument concerns the Canones Hippolyti; it is not a finding on the Apostolic Tradition. He is working in 1891; later work (Dix, Botte, Brent) is not read here.

ref: Achelis 1891, printed p. 217 (the creed of the Canones Hippolyti, third article)
greek: Dass der Zusatz zum dritten Artikel 'procedentem a patre filio que' nicht urspriinglich ist, bedarf trotz Hanebergs Freude uber diese alte Bezeugung der abendlandischen Lehre unter Einsichtigen keines Beweises. Es kann erst der koptischen oder gar arabischen Geschichte der C. H. entstammen.
greek_edition: German, OCR text layer (diecanoneshippol00hipp_djvu.txt; PDF p. 227). Not Greek. Quoted as printed: 'filio que' (OCR space), 'urspriinglich' = ursprünglich, 'Griinde' etc. as OCR.
english: That the addition to the third article, 'proceeding from the Father and the Son' (filioque), is not original needs no proof for informed readers, despite Haneberg's pleasure at this old witness to Western doctrine. It can only derive from the Coptic or even the Arabic history of the Canones Hippolyti.
page: printed p. 217; PDF p. 227 of diecanoneshippol00hipp.pdf
edition: Hans Achelis, Die Canones Hippolyti, Leipzig, 1891
what_it_says: Achelis holds the Western filioque in the Canones creed to be a late addition from the Coptic or Arabic transmission, not the original text.
limits: This is Achelis' opinion about the Canones creed; the AT creed has no filioque in the witnesses read here (Verona, Tattam, Horner, Rahmani). The result is 1891 scholarship, not a manuscript proof.

ref: Apostolic Constitutions, Book VII, ch. 41 (Greek-based church order, not the Apostolic Tradition); ANF 7 ch. numbering 'XLI'
greek_edition: Greek not read (only the English of ANF 7 was read)
english: I associate myself to Christ, and believe, and am baptized into one unbegotten Being, the only true God Almighty, the Father of Christ, the Creator and Maker of all things, from whom are all things; and into the Lord Jesus Christ, His only begotten Son, the First-born of the whole creation, who before the ages was begotten by the good pleasure of the Father, by whom all things were made.
translator: James Donaldson (ANF 7 translation; the newadvent page says 'Translated by James Donaldson')
page: page unknown (ANF 7 print pagination not checked); newadvent ch. XLI
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (Roberts & Donaldson), read on newadvent
what_it_says: The Constitutions' baptismal declaration says 'baptized into one unbegotten Being, the only true God Almighty', then the Son as first-born of creation begotten before the ages, then the Holy Ghost.
limits: This is a declaratory, not interrogatory, creed, from a different document (AC VII), not the Apostolic Tradition. 'Unbegotten Being' is Arian-sensitive wording; the Son's 'begotten before the ages' is in the same text. Whether AC 7 depends on the AT is not decided here.

ref: Eusebius, Historia ecclesiastica 6.22.2 (Chapter 22, 'The Works of Hippolytus which have reached us')
english: Of his other writings the following have reached us: On the Hexæmeron, On the Works after the Hexæmeron, Against Marcion, On the Song of Songs, On Portions of Ezekiel, On the Passover, Against All the Heresies; and you can find many other works preserved by many.
translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1, as shown on newadvent)
page: NPNF2 page not given on newadvent; page unknown
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1, read on newadvent
what_it_says: Eusebius lists Hippolytus' surviving works (Hexaemeron, Marcion, Song of Songs, Passover, Against All the Heresies...) and does not name the Apostolic Tradition or any church order.
limits: Negative result: the list is 'many other works', so the omission is not conclusive. Eusebius' list is the earliest, but it does not say the AT was by Hippolytus or by someone else.

english: He wrote some commentaries on the Scriptures, among which are the following: On the six days of creation, On Exodus, On the Song of Songs, On Genesis, On Zechariah, On the Psalms, On Isaiah, On Daniel, On the Apocalypse, On the Proverbs, On Ecclesiastes, On Saul, On the Pythonissa, On the Antichrist, On the resurrection, Against Marcion, On the Passover, Against all heresies
translator: Ernest Cushing Richardson (NPNF2 vol. 3, as shown on newadvent)
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 3, read on newadvent
what_it_says: Jerome lists Hippolytus' commentaries and works (on Daniel, Genesis, the Psalms, the Passover, Against all heresies, etc.) and says he cannot learn the name of Hippolytus' see. No Apostolic Tradition or church order is named.
limits: Negative result. Jerome's list omits the church order, but also says Hippolytus wrote 'some' works, which is not a complete list. Jerome's statement that the see is unknown is noted but not explained here.

ref: Schaff encyclopedia article 'Hippolytus' (CCEL), section on the statue (Lateran statue, list of works on the seat)
greek_edition: Greek inscription not read; English summary only
english: The statue is dated in the third century by experts. The first lines of the inscription are illegible; the others name nine or ten works, to which two more were added later.
translator: not identified on the CCEL page (author not verified)
edition: CCEL page iii.xi.lxxiii (Schaff encyclopedia, read online)
what_it_says: The Lateran statue (1551) carries a list of Hippolytus' writings in Greek, of which nine or ten survive and two more were added later; the list's wording is not read here.
limits: The Greek list is not read, so it is not known whether the statue names a work identifiable with the Apostolic Tradition (a suggestion in the literature, not verified here). The article is an encyclopedia summary.
